transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 67 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Markus Halvorsen (CTO, Cygnus), Lena Ortiz (ML Eng), Victor Sun (Infra)

00:00 Jordan Lee: ok, thanks everyone for joining uh this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, we'll kick off with a quick agenda, then Priya will jump into the runtime diagrams and perf numbers.
00:28 Markus Halvorsen: hey thanks, Markus here, will try to keep it focused, we've got about an hour plus, mostly interested in the KV side and how lazy append helps our telemetry traces pipeline.
01:02 Priya Raman: awesome. quick note, speakers might be slightly off, fireflies sometimes labels me speaker 2 even when I'm talking, so apologies if that happens.
: (laughter)
01:18 Lena Ortiz: quick context from our side -- we're ingesting multi-hour telemetry blobs, want a single session view up to 128k tokens today, want to explore 256k to 512k for Q3. latency tightness under 200ms p50 generation for short prompts, but long context scoring throughput is key.
01:50 Jordan Lee: good. Priya, could you orient them to the hybrid-tiling idea?
02:12 Priya Raman: sure. slide 1 — hybrid KV-tiling is basically split across two dimensions: a hot-tier per-request in-GPU KV (fast small tiles) and a warm-tier that's sharded across nodes for long prefix fetches. Instead of materializing whole prefix into GPU we stream tiles lazily, append-on-read, which avoids copying entire 500k context.
02:47 Victor Sun: so append-on-read is different from our current append-on-write pattern, correct? we currently materialize then write to S3 and re-hydrate.
03:18 Priya Raman: exactly, append-on-write writes whole state eagerly. lazy-append (or append-on-read) means we only pull tiles that attention touches; also we do prefix bucketing so locality is preserved. there are tradeoffs with extra RPCs.
03:50 Markus Halvorsen: what's the RPC overhead like? our infra team is worried about chatty behavior over VPC peering.
04:12 Priya Raman: we measured median extra RPC latency of 0.8-1.2ms per tile when co-located; across peers it's 2-5ms depending on network egress. that's why we recommend grouping tiles into 64-128KB buckets to amortize RPCs.
04:45 Lena Ortiz: is there a memory tax on GPU? if we keep many hot tiles in-GPU for a long session, will it evict weights or reduce batch concurrency?
05:08 Priya Raman: yes, there's a memory/throughput tradeoff. our runtime uses adaptive eviction: it keeps MRU hot tiles pinned, and when pressure hits we spill LRU tiles to host memory or remote warm-tier. that reduces GPU batch size by about 1-2 tokens per sequence in our tests, not huge but measurable on 80GB nodes.
05:42 Victor Sun: can you show numbers from your 128k->256k runs?
06:05 Priya Raman: sure, pulled from our internal perf sheet: baseline 128k with hybrid-tiling + q4 runs at ~65 tokens/sec sustained on an A100-80GB with 1 client, tail p95 latency for small turns ~180ms. When we scale to 256k without tiling (full materialize) throughput dropped by 70%. With tiling and lazy-append throughput stayed within 20% of 128k baseline.
06:48 Markus Halvorsen: that's promising. what about quantization interplay? we noticed hallucination rates spiking with aggressive q4boost.
07:10 Priya Raman: yes, quantization affects activation dynamics; our recommendation is mixed: use q5_0 weights for decoder stacks, q4 for KV storage if model behavior tolerates it, and keep layernorms in higher precision. We run evals for hallucination/regression on customer prompt sets before recommending aggressive quant.
07:40 Lena Ortiz: any examples of mismatch? like where quantization killed retrieval accuracy?
08:02 Priya Raman: on retrieval tasks with very long prefix concatenation, q4-only KV led to degred of small entity recall around ~3-5% in our internal NER tests. switching KV to q5 improved recall back near baseline.
08:28 Jordan Lee: Markus, do you have constraints on KMS/HSM for on-prem keys? we often see heavy asks about HSM integration.
08:45 Markus Halvorsen: yes, we need HSM-backed keys and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM; also SSO requirements.
09:03 Jordan Lee: we support external KMS and HSM, Redwood Private can integrate with customer KMS; we'll add that to the security docs we send.
09:28 Victor Sun: about the VPC peering, are there specific ports or egress patterns? our security team will want a minimal allowed list.
09:45 Priya Raman: most traffic is GRPC over 443; control-plane calls are occasional. For the warm-tier we recommend secure TCP with mutual TLS, and you can restrict endpoints to the peered subnet. we'll send a config snippet.
10:05 Lena Ortiz: can you talk about eviction policies? LRU vs frequency-based?
10:22 Priya Raman: yes. LRU is simple but can thrash when you have many long but infrequent contexts. We use hybrid LFU-LRU with time-decay (we call it TTL-Freq) — short high-frequency prefixes stay, long tails age out. You can tune decay window per workload.
10:45 Markus Halvorsen: tuning is key for us, since telemetry bursts during incident windows. will auto-eviction be deterministic? we need reproducible behavior for forensics.
11:05 Priya Raman: we log eviction events with sequence IDs and timestamps to the audit log. Reproducibility comes from deterministic policy configs and you can run in 'dry-run' to see what would have been evicted.
11:32 Jordan Lee: quick q from me — how do you handle consistency if a tile is being written while a read happens? race conditions?
11:48 Priya Raman: we use compare-and-swap plus versioned tile IDs. reads see last committed version, in-flight writes stage to a write-ahead buffer. it's eventually consistent within the token micro-batch so generation is stable.
12:10 Victor Sun: that sounds like it may add CPU overhead. what's the CPU vs GPU trade?
12:25 Priya Raman: write path adds some CPU cycles for commit and checksums but it's small; main cost is network. we instrument CPU at about 10-15% utilization on our nodes during heavy lazy pulls.
12:50 Lena Ortiz: what about batching? we have multi-tenant inference so batching across sessions matters.
13:05 Priya Raman: continuous batching works fine; the runtime groups token steps across sessions; hybrid-tiling requires hinting which sessions are likely to touch which tiles so we can prefetch for the batch. We provide a prefetch hint API.
13:35 Markus Halvorsen: can you give a sample prefetch pattern?
13:50 Priya Raman: sample: if you have a call stack that often references last-300 tokens, mark those as high-priority tile keys; the runtime will fetch them into the hot tier before decoding. Works well for conversational workflows.
14:10 Jordan Lee: a bit of transcription noise — someone in the background said "what's the bill" (laughs), will cost be a concern?
14:25 Lena Ortiz: cost is a huge concern. what's the unit economics with hybrid-tiling vs full materialize?
14:40 Priya Raman: short answer: hybrid-tiling reduces per-token GPU time by ~25-40% on long contexts and reduces host memory footprint. But there's a network and control-plane cost; overall TCO depends on request patterns. We'll send a cost model spreadsheet.
15:05 Markus Halvorsen: please do. also include dedicated vs hosted delta.
15:20 Jordan Lee: noted. Priya, can you talk about failure modes — what happens if a tile fetch fails mid-generation?
15:38 Priya Raman: we have graceful fallback: if tile fetch fails, runtime can either fallback to a smaller context window (truncate oldest buckets) or route to a lower-capacity but fully-materialized variant. We surface these events to tracing and we have automated retries.
16:05 Victor Sun: does fallback hurt quality badly?
16:18 Priya Raman: depends on how much of the prefix is lost; in many telemetry summarization tasks losing older context reduces recall but not immediate coherence; but for long instruction-following failures are more visible. We keep customer-specific thresholds.
16:40 Lena Ortiz: you mentioned routing to lower-capacity model variants; how do you keep function-calling parity?
16:55 Priya Raman: we maintain a model family with compatible APIs; variants differ in context capacity and quant but keep tokenizer and function schema identical to avoid breaking downstream logic.
17:18 Markus Halvorsen: show us the benchmark methodology — how do you simulate realistic telemetry loads?
17:35 Priya Raman: we use a generator that emits variable-length traces with burst patterns, mixes short and very long contexts; we record token step time, RPC counts, number of tile fetches, and serialization costs. We also seed with real anonymized traces when customers allow.
18:05 Jordan Lee: can you share a sample artifact after the call?
18:12 Priya Raman: yes, that's in next steps.
18:25 Lena Ortiz: let's talk about quantization again: any safe defaults?
18:38 Priya Raman: safe default: weights in q5_0 across model, KV in q4 if you see no regression on your eval set; embeddings and retrieval indexes in higher precision. Also prefer per-channel quant for layers with high dynamic range.
19:05 Markus Halvorsen: regulatory: do you persist any customer tokens in warm-tier longer than 30 days by default?
19:18 Jordan Lee: default retention is configurable; for Private we can set retention to 0 and only keep ephemeral caches. Audit logs can be stored per customer policy.
19:40 Victor Sun: on the private deployment, do you provide the control plane or do we host all components?
19:55 Priya Raman: Redwood Private provides a minimal control plane; you can run the runtime fully in your VPC or on-prem; control plane components can be run in your environment for air-gapped installs. We provide helm charts.
20:18 Lena Ortiz: any known issues on k8s versions?
20:30 Priya Raman: we support 1.25+ for production. older versions may need tweaks to hugepage settings. We'll include a k8s checklist.
20:50 Jordan Lee: circling back — Markus, what are your success criteria for the POC?
21:05 Markus Halvorsen: 1) sustain 40 tokens/sec for 256k session with 99% of responses under 500ms for small turns, 2) no more than 5% recall degradation vs our offline baseline, 3) run inside our VPC with HSM keys enabled.
21:28 Priya Raman: noted — we'll target those.
21:40 Lena Ortiz: any concerns about model drift when using quantized variants over time?
21:55 Priya Raman: drift is possible; we recommend scheduled evals and automatic rollback if quality metrics slip. Redwood Optimize can run those evals for you.
22:12 Victor Sun: let's talk instrumentation — what traces/logs will we get?
22:25 Priya Raman: token-level timing, per-tile fetch trace, eviction logs, model variant switch logs, and cost attribution per token. All can be forwarded to your logging endpoint or stored in the console.
22:48 Jordan Lee: are there customer examples for telemetry workloads?
23:00 Priya Raman: yes, some early customers in fleet telemetry used a similar hybrid pattern and cut costs by ~30% while keeping acceptable recall. can't name them on the call but we'll include anonymized case study.
23:20 Markus Halvorsen: ok, any open risks?
23:32 Priya Raman: network noisiness and mis-tuned eviction windows are the main ones. Also quantization misconfig if you don't eval on domain prompts.
23:50 Lena Ortiz: what's the recommended process for the POC?
24:02 Jordan Lee: suggested: 1) get access to a single A100-80GB test node in your VPC, 2) Redwood sends prebuilt runtime image and helm chart, 3) Priya's team runs a baseline and then a hybrid-tiling config, 4) compare metrics and tune eviction.
24:28 Markus Halvorsen: timeline? we can spin a node by next week.
24:38 Jordan Lee: great, we'll aim for initial runs by 2027-04-09 and a check-in on 2027-04-13.
24:50 Victor Sun: any notes about security scan? we have a standard pentest pipeline.
25:05 Priya Raman: we can provide an SBOM and point you to our compliance pack; for Private installs we also allow you to run the container through your scanner.
25:20 Lena Ortiz: micro-question — do you support ephemeral cache encryption at rest?
25:33 Priya Raman: yes, both in-host and warm-tier storage can be encrypted using your KMS. we also support in-memory encryption for certain setups.
25:50 Jordan Lee: ok let's surface some concrete numbers from the sheet — Priya?
26:05 Priya Raman: pasted from perf: scenario A (materialize 256k) - baseline tokens/sec 18; scenario B (hybrid-tiling + lazy) - tokens/sec 48; cost per million tokens fell 38% in our estimate.
26:38 Markus Halvorsen: that's a big delta. what's the variance?
26:50 Priya Raman: variance depends on burstiness; during bursts throughput drops as prefetch catches up, so we recommend droppable prefetch windows.
27:10 Lena Ortiz: are you open to a small change: we want deterministic eviction for forensics but also the option to prioritize throughput during incidents.
27:25 Priya Raman: yes, you can flip modes — deterministic vs throughput-optimized — via runtime flags. We also keep an audit trail when mode changes occur.
27:48 Victor Sun: will switching modes cause re-sharding? any downtime?
28:00 Priya Raman: mode changes are soft and applied at new session boundaries; we avoid global re-sharding in day-to-day ops.
28:15 Jordan Lee: question from chat about model warmstart — do you pre-warm embeddings for common tokens?
28:30 Priya Raman: yes, we have a prewarm step for high-frequency buckets; it can be customer-provided list or auto-detected after a warmup window.
28:48 Markus Halvorsen: final thing — legal/procurement notes: we'll want SOC2 attestation and a draft SOW for Private.
29:05 Jordan Lee: we'll attach SOC2 and a draft SOW to the follow-up email.
29:18 Lena Ortiz: cool. any final clarifying q's?
29:30 Markus Halvorsen: none from me. thanks, that was dense and useful.
29:40 Jordan Lee: great, we'll follow up with artifacts and schedule the POC start for next week. thanks everyone.
29:50 (call ends; some chatter)
30:05 End of recording

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-heard words (e.g., "q4boost" vs "Q4 boost"), speaker labels may not perfectly align. Artifacts promised: perf CSV, helm chart, k8s checklist, security pack, cost model spreadsheet.
